en: The Jātaka: The Fifth Book of Birth Stories,
Chapter on the Half-Units (Aḍḍhavagga)
2. The Jātaka of the Little Deer "For you who have departed from the home and are now homeless;..."
"It is not good for a recluse that you grieve for the deceased. "Indeed,
Sakka, through living together..."
Whether it be for a human or a deer,
love arises in the heart;
it is not possible not to grieve for that.
“They weep for the dead and they weep for those about to die;
therefore, O seer, do not weep.”
The virtuous say that weeping is in vain.
For by weeping, O Brahmā,
could a dead person who has passed away be raised up?
"Let us all come together and weep for our respective kinsmen. "Alas,
while I am burning, [you do not see it]."
Like a fire drenched with a jar of water, by sprinkling it with water,
one should extinguish every affliction.
Truly, pull out the arrow that was lodged in my heart,
you who [have done so] for me while I was overcome by grief.
I have dispelled the grief for my son.
I am one whose dart has been pulled out,
free from sorrow and undisturbed.
“I do not grieve, nor do I weep,
having heard this from you, O Vāsava.
Thus ends the second Jātaka, the Migapotaka-jātaka.
